reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Produces abnormal posturing or spasm only during a particular skilled, often over-practised, motor task
Writer's cramp and musician's dystonia are the classic examples; embouchure dystonia and the sporting yips are others
The same muscles function normally during other activities, which is the defining feature
Symptoms often begin as loss of fine control or cramping and progress to overt posturing as the task continues
A sensory trick may temporarily relieve the dystonia in some patients
It typically affects adults engaged in repetitive precision tasks and can be occupationally disabling
Over time the dystonia may spread to related tasks, with loss of the original task specificity
reference.pathophysiology: Task-specific focal dystonia is thought to arise from maladaptive plasticity within the sensorimotor system, with reduced inhibition at cortical, subcortical and spinal levels and abnormal integration of sensory feedback with motor output. Extensive repetitive practice of a skilled task appears to drive aberrant cortical reorganisation that blurs the normally distinct representations of individual digits or muscles, so that performing the specific over-learned movement triggers involuntary co-contraction and abnormal posturing.
additionalDifferentials: Overuse or repetitive strain injury and tenosynovitis
Peripheral nerve entrapment or focal neuropathy
Early features of a generalised or secondary dystonia
Orthopaedic or musculoskeletal disorders of the hand
additionalInvestigations: Task-based clinical examination, ideally observing the patient performing the triggering activity such as writing or playing an instrument
Surface electromyography demonstrating co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles
Nerve conduction studies to exclude focal neuropathy or entrapment
MRI where a structural or secondary cause is suspected
Copper studies and genetic testing in younger patients or those with wider features
Video recording of the task to document and monitor the dystonia
redFlags: Dystonia at rest or spreading beyond the specific task, suggesting a secondary or generalising process
Sensory loss, weakness or wasting suggesting a compressive or neuropathic lesion
Young onset with additional neurological features suggesting an inherited dystonia
Features of Wilson's disease in a younger patient
reference.prognosis: Task-specific dystonia is generally chronic and spontaneous remission is uncommon, though severity can fluctuate. It is not life-threatening but may curtail or end a career dependent on the affected skill. Botulinum toxin injection targeted to the overactive muscles is a mainstay of treatment, and some patients benefit from retraining, ergonomic modification or a change of technique, with results that vary between individuals.
pitfalls: Dismissing early symptoms as overuse injury or anxiety
Not observing the patient performing the actual triggering task
Neglecting the occupational and psychological impact
Assuming permanent task specificity, when the dystonia can spread to related tasks
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice, current edition
Fahn and Jankovic, Principles and Practice of Movement Disorders
management: Use botulinum toxin injection targeted to the overactive muscles as the mainstay of treatment
Modify the triggering task with ergonomic aids, altered technique, grip adaptations or switching to the other hand
Provide sensorimotor retraining and physiotherapy, including constraint and rehabilitation strategies to restore normal control
Trial oral anticholinergic therapy such as trihexyphenidyl in selected patients
Teach use of any effective sensory trick to relieve posturing
Consider copper studies and genetic testing in younger patients or those with wider dystonic features
Refer to neurology with movement-disorder expertise and involve occupational or performing-arts medicine support
